learn.hook: Plans are ready, teams are formed, people are hired. But nothing moves until someone says 'Let's go!' Directing is the spark that starts the engine.
points: Directing means instructing, guiding, communicating with and inspiring people in the organisation to achieve its objectives.
Characteristics: directing initiates action; takes place at every level of management (pervasive); is a continuous process; and flows from top to bottom (a manager directs subordinates).

Importance: initiates action; integrates employees' efforts towards common goals; is a means of motivation; facilitates implementation of changes (by reducing resistance through communication and motivation); and brings stability and balance in the organisation.
Elements of directing: supervision, motivation, leadership and communication.

example.q: When Nirmal Foods decided to shift to automated packing, its managers explained the benefits, trained workers and assured job security, so the change went smoothly. Which importance of directing is shown?
steps: Workers usually resist change.
Managers used communication and motivation to reduce resistance.
This shows directing facilitates implementation of changes.

learn.reallife: A railway station master guiding staff during a festival rush, through instructions, encouragement and quick communication, is directing in action.

games.title: Match the feature or importance
pairs: Links individual work to common goals

quiz.explain: These are the core activities of directing.

quiz.explain: Directing happens wherever there is a superior-subordinate relationship.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an element of directing?
quiz.explain: Recruitment belongs to staffing.

quiz.explain: Leaders and managers align individual work with common goals.

quiz.q: Plans and structures of Sagar Ltd were ready, but work began only after managers gave instructions. Which importance of directing is shown?
quiz.explain: Directing is the function that starts actual work.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Because it goes on throughout the organisation's life, it is continuous. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks directing stops once work begins

quiz.q: Through leadership, communication and motivation, directing helps balance different interests and keeps the organisation steady. This is:
quiz.explain: Balancing interests brings stability.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is initiation of action

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Everything is planned. Why does anyone need to direct?'
teach.praise: Plans need a push! Directing instructs, guides and inspires, and starts the action.
teach.nudge: A plan can't move itself. What does directing do to get people working?

learn.hook: A supervisor in a garment unit settles a quarrel, teaches a new stitch and passes a worker's idea to the manager, all before lunch. That is supervision.
points: Principles of directing: maximum individual contribution; harmony of objectives (individual and organisational goals should match); unity of command; appropriateness of direction technique (suited to subordinates' needs and abilities); managerial communication (clear, and understood as intended); use of informal organisation; leadership; and follow-through (checking whether instructions are being implemented).
Supervision means overseeing subordinates at work. Its meaning varies with the level, but it is especially important at the first line (supervisory) level.

Role or importance of a supervisor: maintains day-to-day contact and friendly relations with workers; acts as a link between workers and management (link pin); maintains group unity by settling disputes; ensures work is done as per targets; provides on-the-job training; builds positive attitudes through leadership; and analyses work and gives feedback.

example.q: Supervisor Imran notices two workers quarrelling over shift timings. He talks to both and settles the matter so the team works well again. Which role is shown?
steps: The workers were in conflict.
The supervisor settled their dispute.
This is maintaining group unity.

learn.reallife: Station supervisors on Indian Railways guide staff, train new porters and report problems upward, the classic link-pin role of supervision.

games.title: Match the principle of directing
pairs: Using informal groups for effective direction

games.title: Supervisor's role
items: A supervisor acts as a link between workers and management.
A supervisor settles internal disputes to maintain group unity.
That is part of the role.
Supervision is relevant only at the top level.
It is especially important at the operational level.

quiz.q: Which principle of directing requires that individual and organisational objectives should match?
quiz.explain: Harmony means individual goals support organisational goals.
quiz.mistake: Confuses harmony with unity of command

quiz.q: Checking whether instructions given to subordinates are being implemented is the principle of:
quiz.explain: Follow-through means monitoring implementation.

quiz.q: A manager uses employees' informal groups to spread positive information about a change. Which principle is applied?
quiz.explain: Effective directors use informal groups wisely.

quiz.q: Supervision means:
quiz.explain: Supervision is watching and guiding work as it happens.

quiz.q: Why is a supervisor called a 'link pin'?
options: Because the supervisor sets company policy
Because the supervisor owns the company
Because the supervisor links workers with management
quiz.explain: Supervisors convey management's ideas to workers and workers' problems to management.
quiz.mistake: Thinks link pin means top manager

quiz.q: Supervisor Latha teaches a new worker how to operate the cutting machine on the shop floor. This shows the supervisor's role in:
quiz.explain: Supervisors train workers on the job.

quiz.q: A manager chooses a motivating style for experienced staff and closer guidance for new staff. Which principle is applied?
quiz.explain: The technique is suited to subordinates' needs and abilities.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is maximum individual contribution

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A supervisor helps maintain group unity among workers. Reason (R): A supervisor settles internal disputes among workers.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Settling disputes keeps the group united. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks disputes are management's problem only

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does a supervisor actually do all day?'
teach.praise: Oversees work, links workers with management, settles disputes and trains people. Busy bird!
teach.nudge: Think of who the supervisor connects, and what she does for workers on the floor.

topics.title: Motivation: meaning, features, process and importance

learn.hook: Why does one salesperson make 50 calls a day and another only 10, with the same salary? The answer is motivation.
points: Motive: an inner state that energises, activates or moves and directs behaviour towards goals. Motivation: the process of stimulating people to action to accomplish desired goals. Motivators: the techniques used to motivate people, e.g. pay, bonus, promotion, recognition.

Features: motivation is an internal feeling; it produces goal-directed behaviour; it can be positive (rewards, promotion) or negative (punishment, stopping increments); it is a complex process because people differ in needs and reactions.
Process: unsatisfied need → tension → drives → search behaviour → satisfied need → reduction of tension.
Importance: improves performance; changes negative or indifferent attitudes to positive ones; reduces employee turnover; reduces absenteeism; helps introduce changes smoothly.

example.q: Neha wants a promotion. She feels restless, so she joins an evening course and takes on extra projects. After she is promoted, she feels at ease. Map this to the motivation process.
steps: Unsatisfied need: promotion
Tension: restlessness
Drive and search behaviour: course and extra projects
Satisfied need: promotion achieved
Reduction of tension: she feels at ease
example.answer: Unsatisfied need → tension → drive → search behaviour → satisfied need → reduced tension

learn.reallife: Sales leaderboards and 'employee of the month' boards in Indian retail chains use positive motivation to raise performance.

games.title: Motivation process
games.prompt: Arrange the motivation process in order

games.title: Match the term
pairs: Process of stimulating people to act

quiz.q: An inner state that energises, activates and directs behaviour towards goals is called:
quiz.explain: A motive is the internal force; motivators are the techniques used.

quiz.q: Pay, bonus, promotion and recognition used to motivate people are called:
quiz.explain: These are techniques or tools of motivation.

quiz.q: What comes immediately after 'unsatisfied need' in the motivation process?
quiz.explain: An unsatisfied need creates tension first.

quiz.q: Stopping an employee's increment for poor work is an example of:
quiz.explain: Punishment-based motivation is negative.

quiz.q: Why is motivation called a complex process?
options: Because only top managers can do it
Because individuals differ in their needs and responses
quiz.explain: Different people react differently to the same motivator.

quiz.q: Which is an importance of motivation?
options: It removes the need for supervision
It reduces employee turnover and absenteeism
quiz.explain: Motivated employees stay longer and attend regularly.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Motivation is an internal feeling. Reason (R): Urges, drives and needs of human beings are internal, and they influence behaviour.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Motivation comes from inner needs and drives. R explains A.

quiz.q: Bharat Tools offered recognition to motivated workers, and even indifferent workers became positive about their work. Which importance of motivation is shown?
options: Changes negative or indifferent attitudes to positive ones
quiz.explain: Motivation can turn indifferent attitudes positive.

teach.ask: Gappu yawns: 'Why should I try harder if I already get my seeds?'
teach.praise: So an unsatisfied need creates tension, I search and act, and once it's met the tension goes. Now I want more than seeds!
teach.nudge: What starts the whole motivation process inside a person? Think about needs and tension.

learn.hook: First you need food, then a safe room, then friends, then respect, and finally the chance to become your best self. Maslow arranged our needs like a staircase.
points: Abraham Maslow's need hierarchy has five levels, from lowest to highest: physiological, safety or security, affiliation or belonging (social), esteem, and self-actualisation.

Physiological needs: basic survival needs like food, water, shelter and sleep; met through basic salary. Safety needs: physical and economic security, e.g. job security, stability of income, pension plans.
Affiliation or belonging needs: affection, sense of belonging, acceptance and friendship. Esteem needs: self-respect, autonomy, status, recognition and attention.
Self-actualisation: the highest need, to become what one is capable of becoming, including growth, self-fulfilment and achievement of goals.
Assumptions: behaviour depends on needs; needs are in a hierarchical order; a satisfied need no longer motivates; a person moves to the next higher level only when the lower need is satisfied.

example.q: Identify the need: (i) Ravi wants a permanent job with a pension. (ii) Priya wants to be named 'Best Designer' at the annual meet. (iii) Arjun wants to start his own research lab to fulfil his potential.
steps: (i) Job security and pension = safety needs
(ii) Recognition and status = esteem needs
(iii) Reaching one's full potential = self-actualisation

learn.reallife: A daily-wage worker first seeks enough pay for food and shelter (physiological), then a permanent job with a steady income (safety). A top scientist at ISRO may be driven by self-actualisation.

games.title: Maslow's hierarchy
games.prompt: Arrange from the lowest need to the highest

games.title: Match the need to its example
pairs: Basic salary for food and shelter
Becoming what one is capable of

quiz.explain: Self-actualisation is the top of the hierarchy.

quiz.explain: These are social needs.

quiz.explain: Esteem covers respect, status and recognition.

quiz.explain: Food and shelter are basic survival needs.

quiz.q: Kabir, a software engineer, has a good salary, secure job, friends and a senior title. He now wants to build an app that he believes in. According to Maslow, which need is motivating him?
quiz.explain: With lower needs met, he seeks to fulfil his potential.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a senior title still motivates him

quiz.q: Which is an assumption of Maslow's theory?
options: All needs motivate equally at the same time
Higher needs must be met before lower ones
A satisfied need no longer motivates a person
quiz.explain: Once satisfied, a need stops motivating; the next higher one takes over.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A person moves to the next higher level of the hierarchy only when the lower need is satisfied. Reason (R): According to Maslow, human needs are arranged in a hierarchical order.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because needs are in a hierarchy, they are met from lower to higher. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks needs can be met in any order

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does Maslow's staircase look like from the bottom step?'
teach.praise: Food, safety, friends, respect and then my best self. I'm climbing Maslow's staircase!
teach.nudge: Start at the bottom step. What does everyone need first, and what comes next?

learn.hook: Money talks, but so does a thank-you, a challenging project and a say in decisions. Smart firms use both kinds of incentives.
points: Financial incentives are direct or indirect monetary rewards: pay and allowances (salary, dearness allowance, increments); productivity-linked wage incentives; bonus (over and above wages); profit sharing; co-partnership or stock option (shares offered to employees at a price lower than the market price); retirement benefits (provident fund, pension, gratuity); perquisites (car, housing, medical aid, children's education).

Non-financial incentives satisfy psychological, social and emotional needs: status (rank of positions); organisational climate (e.g. autonomy, rewarding orientation, concern for employees); career advancement opportunity; job enrichment (more variety, higher knowledge and skills, more autonomy and responsibility in the job); employee recognition programmes; job security; employee participation (e.g. joint management committees, work committees, canteen committees, suggestion programmes); and employee empowerment (more autonomy and powers to subordinates).
Financial incentives mainly satisfy lower-level needs; non-financial incentives mainly satisfy higher-level needs like esteem and self-actualisation.

example.q: Classify: (i) A company offers its shares to staff at a lower price than the market price. (ii) A worker's job is redesigned to include planning and quality checks, giving her more responsibility.
steps: (i) Shares at a concessional price = co-partnership or stock option (financial)
(ii) More variety, skills and autonomy in the job = job enrichment (non-financial)

learn.reallife: Many Indian startups give ESOPs (employee stock options) to retain talent, a financial incentive, while also offering flexible roles and recognition, which are non-financial.

games.title: Match the incentive
pairs: Company car, housing and medical aid
More variety and autonomy in the job
Rank or position in the organisation

quiz.q: Which of these is a financial incentive?
quiz.explain: Profit sharing gives employees a share in profits, a monetary reward.

quiz.q: Offering shares to employees at a price lower than the market price is called:
quiz.explain: This makes employees part-owners at a concession.

quiz.q: Designing jobs with greater variety, higher skills, more autonomy and responsibility is:
quiz.explain: Job enrichment makes work more challenging and meaningful.

quiz.q: Car, housing, medical aid and education for children provided by an employer are:
quiz.explain: These are perks over and above salary.

quiz.q: Giving subordinates more autonomy and powers is a non-financial incentive called:
quiz.explain: Empowerment means more freedom and power to act.

quiz.q: Nova Textiles includes worker representatives on its canteen and safety committees. Which incentive is this?
quiz.explain: Involving workers in decisions through committees is participation.

quiz.q: Provident fund, pension and gratuity are examples of:
quiz.explain: These are financial benefits given on retirement.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Non-financial incentives are important for motivating employees. Reason (R): Employees have psychological, social and emotional needs that money alone cannot satisfy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Since money cannot meet all needs, non-financial incentives are needed. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks money is the only motivator

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Isn't money the only thing that makes people work hard?'
teach.praise: Money helps, but recognition, enriched jobs and a say in decisions motivate too!
teach.nudge: Money is one kind. What are some non-money incentives a company can give?

learn.hook: One captain barks orders, another discusses field placements, a third lets senior players decide. Three different leadership styles, and each can work in the right setting.
points: Leadership is the process of influencing the behaviour of people by making them strive voluntarily towards achieving organisational goals.

Features: it is an ability to influence others; it tries to bring change in people's behaviour; it shows the interpersonal relation between leader and followers; it is exercised to achieve common goals; it is a continuous process.
Importance: influences behaviour; maintains personal relations and helps followers meet their needs; introduces required changes; handles conflicts; prepares successors through training.

Styles based on use of authority: autocratic or authoritarian (gives orders and expects compliance; decisions centralised; one-way communication; useful for quick decisions or when subordinates need close supervision); democratic or participative (decides in consultation with subordinates; two-way communication; encourages participation); laissez-faire or free-rein (gives subordinates high independence; leader mainly supports; suits competent and responsible subordinates).

example.q: Identify the style: (i) Captain Rana decides every field placement himself and allows no discussion. (ii) Manager Sana asks her team for ideas before finalising a plan. (iii) Professor Iyer lets her expert researchers set their own goals and methods.
steps: (i) Orders with no consultation = autocratic
(ii) Consultation and participation = democratic
(iii) High independence to experts = laissez-faire

learn.reallife: In disaster relief, such as during floods, quick autocratic decisions may save lives, while research labs often prefer a free-rein style.

games.title: Which leadership style?

games.title: Leadership true or false

quiz.q: Leadership is best described as:
options: Forcing people to work through penalties

quiz.explain: Leadership relies on influence, not force.
quiz.mistake: Thinks leadership is control by fear

quiz.q: A leader who centralises decisions and expects strict compliance follows the:
quiz.explain: Autocratic leaders command and expect obedience.

quiz.q: Which style involves taking decisions in consultation with subordinates?
quiz.explain: Democratic leaders encourage participation.

quiz.q: Dr Mehra lets his team of experienced scientists set their own work plans and only steps in when asked. His style is:
quiz.explain: High independence to competent subordinates marks free-rein leadership.

quiz.q: Which situation best suits the autocratic style?
options: When subordinates are highly skilled experts
When the team sets its own goals
When quick decisions are needed and subordinates need close supervision
quiz.explain: Autocratic style allows fast decisions with less consultation.
quiz.mistake: Picks a situation suited to free-rein

quiz.q: Leadership helps resolve disagreements among team members. This importance is:
quiz.explain: Leaders manage conflicts effectively.

quiz.q: Which is a feature of leadership?
options: It is exercised only through punishment
It shows the interpersonal relation between leader and followers
It has no link with goals
quiz.explain: Leadership is a relationship between leader and followers.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Democratic leadership encourages employees to participate in decision making. Reason (R): A democratic leader develops action plans and makes decisions in consultation with subordinates.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Consultation is how participation happens. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Should a leader bark orders, ask everyone, or just let us fly free?'
teach.praise: It depends! Autocratic for quick calls, democratic for teamwork, laissez-faire for experts. Tweet!
teach.nudge: Can you name the three styles and when each one works best?

learn.hook: A manager sends a WhatsApp message: 'Meet at 5.' Half the team comes at 5 a.m. Communication is not just sending; it is being understood.
points: Communication is the process of exchange of ideas, views, facts and feelings between two or more persons to create a common understanding.

Elements: sender (conveys the message), message (content of ideas or feelings), encoding (converting the message into words, symbols or gestures), media (the path: face-to-face, phone, email, letter), decoding (converting the symbols back into meaning), receiver (who gets the message), feedback (receiver's response showing the message was understood) and noise (any obstruction or hindrance, e.g. poor phone line, inattention, ambiguous symbols).

Importance: basis of coordination; helps smooth working of the enterprise; basis of decision making; increases managerial efficiency; promotes cooperation and industrial peace; establishes effective leadership; boosts morale and provides motivation.

example.q: Manager Joseph writes an email to his team in simple Hindi and English; the team reads it, understands it and replies 'Noted, will do'. Identify encoding, media, decoding and feedback.
steps: Encoding: putting his ideas into simple Hindi and English words
Media: email
Decoding: the team reading and understanding the words
Feedback: the reply 'Noted, will do'
example.answer: Encoding = writing in words; media = email; decoding = understanding; feedback = reply

learn.reallife: In an ISRO mission control room, clear communication of every command, and confirmation that it was received, can decide mission success.

games.title: The communication process
games.prompt: Arrange the elements in the order they occur

games.title: Match the element
pairs: Converting the message into symbols or words
Path through which the message travels

quiz.q: Communication is the process of exchanging ideas and feelings to create:
quiz.explain: The aim is that both sides understand the same meaning.
quiz.mistake: Thinks communication is just sending information

quiz.q: Converting the message into words, symbols or gestures is called:
quiz.explain: Encoding happens at the sender's end.

quiz.q: The receiver's response that shows the message was understood is:
quiz.explain: Feedback completes the communication loop.

quiz.q: A poor phone connection that disturbs a conversation is an example of:
quiz.explain: Any obstruction in communication is noise.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the phone line is only media

quiz.q: Email, letters and phone calls are examples of:
quiz.explain: Media is the path through which the encoded message travels.

quiz.q: Which is an importance of communication?
options: It removes the need for leadership
It acts as the basis of coordination
quiz.explain: Communication links departments and people, enabling coordination.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Communication promotes cooperation and industrial peace. Reason (R): Two-way communication helps management and workers understand each other.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Mutual understanding reduces conflict and builds cooperation. R explains A.

quiz.q: Converting the received symbols back into meaning is done by the receiver through:
quiz.explain: Decoding happens at the receiver's end.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'I chirped a message to my friend but he understood something else. What went wrong?'
teach.praise: Maybe my encoding was unclear, or there was noise! And I should have asked for feedback.
teach.nudge: Think about the steps between the sender and receiver. Where could it have gone wrong?

learn.hook: The official circular says the office will shift next month. But everyone already knew from the lunch-time grapevine last week!
points: Formal communication follows the official chain of command. Vertical: downward (superior to subordinate, e.g. orders, notices, circulars) and upward (subordinate to superior, e.g. leave applications, grievances, suggestions). Horizontal or lateral: between people at the same level in different departments, e.g. production manager and marketing manager.

Formal networks: single chain (from a superior to a subordinate through a chain, one link at a time), wheel (all subordinates communicate through one superior at the centre), circular (each person communicates with neighbours; slow), free flow (everyone communicates with everyone; fast) and inverted V (a subordinate may communicate with the immediate superior and also with the superior's superior, in a limited way).

Informal communication (grapevine) arises from social interaction, without following official channels. Grapevine networks: single strand (each person tells one other in a sequence), gossip (one person tells everyone non-selectively), probability (a person tells others at random) and cluster (a person tells only those he or she trusts).

Formal vs informal: formal follows the scalar chain, is slower, keeps records and is official; informal follows no fixed path, spreads fast, may distort information and has no records. Managers can use the grapevine to spread useful information and get feedback.

example.q: At Bloom Ltd, every regional manager reports to and receives instructions from the national sales head only; they don't talk to each other. Which network is this?
steps: All communication passes through one central person.
The others do not communicate directly with each other.
This is the wheel network.

learn.reallife: Office WhatsApp groups often act as a modern grapevine where news spreads faster than any official memo.

games.title: Formal or informal communication?
items: Spreads very fast with no fixed path

games.title: Match the network
pairs: Message passes down one link at a time

quiz.q: A leave application sent by an employee to the manager is an example of:
quiz.explain: It goes from subordinate to superior through official channels.

quiz.q: Communication between the production manager and the marketing manager is:
quiz.explain: It is between people at the same level in different departments.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all manager communication is vertical

quiz.q: In which formal network does everyone communicate freely with everyone else?
quiz.explain: Free flow allows communication in all directions; it is fastest.

quiz.q: In which formal network is communication slowest because each person talks only to neighbours?
quiz.explain: In a circular network, messages move slowly around the circle.

quiz.q: A person who passes information only to those he or she trusts is using the:
quiz.explain: Cluster spreads through trusted individuals.

quiz.q: Which grapevine network involves one person communicating with others at random?
quiz.explain: Random sharing is the probability network.

quiz.q: Which is a feature of informal communication?
options: It follows the scalar chain strictly
It is slower than formal communication
It spreads fast but may distort information
quiz.explain: Grapevine is quick but can spread rumours.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Managers should completely ban the grapevine. Reason (R): The grapevine can be used by managers to spread useful information and get feedback from employees.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Banning it is neither possible nor wise, so A is false; R is true.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the grapevine only causes harm

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does gossip travel faster than the official notice?'
teach.praise: Formal goes through official channels; the grapevine has no fixed path, so it zooms! But it can twist the truth.
teach.nudge: Compare the two: which one follows the chain of command, and which one has no fixed path?

learn.hook: The boss says 'This report is quite good.' One worker hears praise, another hears criticism. Somewhere a barrier is hiding.
points: Semantic barriers (problems in encoding and decoding): badly expressed message; symbols or words with different meanings (e.g. 'value' can mean price, worth or importance); faulty translations; unclarified assumptions; technical jargon; misreading body language and gestures.

Psychological or emotional barriers: premature evaluation (judging before hearing fully); lack of attention; loss by transmission and poor retention (information is lost as it passes through many people); distrust between sender and receiver.

Organisational barriers: organisational policy (if it does not support free flow); rules and regulations (rigid, time-consuming routes); status (status-conscious managers keep distance); complexity in organisation structure (more levels cause delay and distortion); lack of organisational facilities (meetings, suggestion boxes, open-door policy).

Personal barriers: fear of challenge to authority (a superior withholds information); lack of confidence of the superior in subordinates; unwillingness to communicate (subordinates fear it may hurt them); lack of proper incentives for communication.

example.q: A manager tells a new worker to 'check the BOM against the WIP before the QC run'. The worker looks blank. Which barrier is this?
steps: The words are technical short forms.
The receiver does not understand them.
This is technical jargon, a semantic barrier.

learn.reallife: In many multilingual Indian workplaces, poor translation of circulars between languages leads to confusion, a classic semantic barrier.

games.title: Which type of barrier?
items: Too many levels in the structure

games.title: Match the barrier to the case
pairs: Boss hides information to protect position
Listener is busy with his phone
Senior manager won't talk to juniors
Sender assumes the receiver knows the context

quiz.q: Which of these is a semantic barrier?
quiz.explain: Translation problems affect encoding and decoding of meaning.

quiz.q: Judging the meaning of a message before the sender completes it is:
quiz.explain: Evaluating too early is a psychological barrier.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with lack of attention

quiz.q: When information passes through many levels and loses accuracy, the barrier is:
options: Loss by transmission and poor retention
quiz.explain: Successive transfers lose part of the message.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is an organisational barrier only

quiz.q: A status-conscious manager keeps a distance from subordinates, so they don't share problems. This is a(n):
quiz.explain: Status is listed among organisational barriers.
quiz.mistake: Thinks status is a personal barrier

quiz.q: A superior withholds information because he fears it may reduce his authority. This is a:
quiz.explain: Fear of challenge to authority is a personal barrier.

quiz.q: The word 'value' used in 'What is the value of this ring?' and 'I value our friendship' shows the barrier of:
quiz.explain: One word can carry several meanings.

quiz.q: Subordinates avoid sharing problems because they fear it will hurt their image. This is:
quiz.explain: Unwillingness to communicate is a personal barrier.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Complexity in organisation structure is a barrier to communication. Reason (R): When there are many managerial levels, communication gets delayed and distorted.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: More levels mean more filtering and delay. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'Why do messages get mixed up even when everyone speaks the same language?'
teach.praise: Words, emotions, the structure and people themselves can all block a message. Barriers everywhere!
teach.nudge: Think of the four types: problems with words, with feelings, with the organisation, and with people.

topics.title: Improving communication and directing case studies

learn.hook: Great communicators aren't born; they follow simple habits: think before speaking, listen well and check understanding.
points: Measures to improve communication: clarify the ideas before communicating; communicate according to the needs of the receiver; consult others before communicating; be aware of the language, tone and content of the message; convey things of help and value to the listener; ensure proper feedback; communicate for the present as well as the future; follow up communications; be a good listener.

Case-based questions in directing ask you to identify: an element (supervision, motivation, leadership, communication), a principle of directing, a need level (Maslow), an incentive (financial or non-financial), a leadership style or a communication barrier.
Tip for cases: look for the key clue words, e.g. 'pension' → safety need; 'shares below market price' → stock option; 'consults the team' → democratic; 'jargon' → semantic barrier.

example.q: Manager Asha notices her team often misunderstands instructions. She now writes clear points, avoids jargon and asks each person to repeat the task. Which measures is she using?
steps: Writing clear points: clarify ideas before communicating
Avoiding jargon: communicate according to the receiver's needs
Asking them to repeat the task: ensure proper feedback
example.answer: Clarifying ideas, suiting the receiver and ensuring feedback

learn.reallife: Customer-care teams at Indian telecom firms are trained to listen patiently and repeat the customer's complaint before acting, ensuring feedback.

games.title: Match the measure to the action
pairs: Think through the message before speaking
Ask the receiver to repeat the instruction
Pay patient attention to the other person
Check later whether the instruction was carried out
Involve those concerned while planning the message

games.title: Case clue check
items: A worker wanting a permanent job with pension shows a safety need.
Job security and pension are safety needs.
Offering shares to employees below market price is a non-financial incentive.
It is co-partnership or stock option, a financial incentive.
A manager who consults the team before deciding is democratic.
Technical jargon is a psychological barrier.
Asking the receiver to repeat the message helps ensure feedback.

quiz.q: Which measure improves communication by checking that the message has been understood?
quiz.explain: Feedback confirms understanding.
quiz.mistake: Thinks written messages need no feedback

quiz.q: Before speaking, a manager thinks through what she wants to say. Which measure is this?
quiz.explain: Clear thinking leads to clear messages.

quiz.q: At Surya Ltd, senior employees are given the right to buy company shares at a lower price. Identify the incentive.
quiz.explain: Shares at a concessional price are a stock option.

quiz.q: A supervisor feels a worker is lying even before he finishes his explanation, so she ignores him. Which barrier is this?
quiz.explain: Judging too early and distrust are psychological barriers.

quiz.q: Pooja, who has a good salary, job security and friends at work, now wants recognition for her work. Which need is active?
quiz.explain: Recognition and status are esteem needs.

quiz.q: A manager gives orders and expects them to be followed without question in an emergency. Which style is this?
quiz.explain: Commanding and expecting compliance is autocratic.

quiz.q: Which measure suggests that a manager should check later whether the instructions given were carried out?
quiz.explain: Follow-up ensures action and removes hurdles.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Being a good listener improves communication. Reason (R): Patient and attentive listening solves half the problems of communication.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Listening well reduces misunderstanding. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I make sure my flock understands me the first time?'
teach.praise: Think clearly, suit the listener, ask for feedback and listen well. My flock will finally get it!
teach.nudge: What could you do before speaking, and how would you check they understood?
